title: Islam: remembrance
hook: in the remembrance of God hearts find rest (Quran 13:28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: salat, the five daily prayers. Your line was five pauses. How many did you manage? Day two hundred sixty-nine.

It's two in the morning and your mind won't stop. It replays the conversation from lunch, rehearses tomorrow's meeting, lists everything that could go wrong. You try to push the thoughts away and they come back louder. Anyone who has lain awake like that knows the heart can be the least restful place in the body. Now picture an old man in a mosque after the dawn prayer, beads slipping through his fingers, lips moving softly, the same few words again and again. He looks like the most rested person in the city. Today, on our visit to Islam: dhikr, remembrance.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, MIND RACING.` → `BEADS AFTER THE DAWN PRAYER.` → `DHIKR.`

segments.voice: Dhikr means remembrance, and also mention: to remember God, and to say God's name. The Qur'an asks for it often. One of its best-loved lines, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation, is today's: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Hearts find rest. Not by solving everything, but by remembering. Another verse turns it into a two-way street: remember me, God says, and I will remember you. The simplest dhikr is short phrases. After each daily prayer, many Muslims say subhanallah, glory be to God, thirty-three times; alhamdulillah, praise be to God, thirty-three times; and Allahu akbar, God is greater, thirty-four times, counting on their fingers or on prayer beads called a misbaha or tasbih. A hadith tells that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught this to his daughter Fatima when she was exhausted from hard work and asked for a servant. He told her these words would be better for her than a servant. Dhikr can be silent or aloud, alone or together. Among Sufis, the mystical tradition within Islam, groups gather to chant God's names in rhythm, sometimes for hours, and some Sufi orders pair the words with the breath or with movement. Many Muslims keep a quiet dhikr going through the day: a phrase while waiting for the bus, while walking, while falling asleep. The idea is that the heart is always remembering something. Dhikr gives it something to remember that can hold its weight.
screen: `DHIKR — REMEMBRANCE, MENTION.` · `IN REMEMBRANCE, HEARTS FIND REST.` · `THIRTY-THREE, THIRTY-THREE, THIRTY-FOUR.` · `SILENT OR ALOUD, ALONE OR TOGETHER.` · then, large: `HEARTS FIND REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat one word slowly. Choose a word that settles you. If you're Muslim, it might be Allah, or alhamdulillah. If not, it can be peace, or here, or thank you. Breathe in. On the out-breath, say the word, silently or softly. Again. Again. When the mind runs off, don't scold it. Just return to the word. The bell holds the time.
Dhikr. Remembrance: short phrases said again and again, so that, as the Qur'an says, hearts find rest. Today's word.
Your line: hearts find rest. Tonight, if your mind starts racing, go back to your one word, and let it carry you toward sleep. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: After each daily prayer many Muslims say subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar on their fingers or prayer beads, and Sufi communities gather for dhikr sessions of chanted remembrance.

options: a few phrases to say after prayer.
fork.reveal: the hadith says he taught her subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar, better for her than a servant.

trapdoor: what you thought: repeating words on beads.
what it means: remembering God through short phrases, so the heart can rest.
what a scholar hears: the root dh-k-r, remember and mention; Qur'an 13:28 and 2:152; the 'tasbih of Fatima' in Sahih al-Bukhari.
